The LGV lemma (Lindström–Gessel–Viennot): in a DAG, take starts A1 … Ak and ends B1 … Bk, and let e(Ai, Bj) = number of paths from Ai to Bj. Then det[e(Ai, Bj)] = Σ over vertex-disjoint path systems of sign(σ), where σ says which start goes to which end.

On a grid moving only right / down with starts and ends in "compatible order" (sorted the same way along a diagonal), every disjoint system uses the identity σ, so the determinant counts the non- intersecting path systems exactly (P6657). Grid path counts are binomials: C(dx + dy, dx).

Order matters: if the i-th start is not "left of" the (i+1)-th in the same sense as the ends, crossing systems get sign −1 and the determinant is no longer a count (it can even be negative). Sort starts and ends consistently along the boundary first.
Pentagonal number theorem; O(n√n).

The partition number p(n) (整数划分) counts ways to write n as an unordered sum of positive integers. The simple DP "coins 1 … n" (进阶篇第13章) is O(n²). Euler's pentagonal number theorem: Π (1 − xk) = Σj (−1)j xj(3j−1)/2, so p(n) = Σj≥1 (−1)j+1 (p(n − j(3j−1)/2) + p(n − j(3j+1)/2)): only O(√n) terms each, O(n√n) total.

The generalised pentagonal numbers 1, 2, 5, 7, 12, 15, … come in pairs with signs + +, − −, + +, …. Partitions into distinct parts, or parts with bounds, use similar generating-function tricks (跑步 P6189 has n = 10⁵).

Ranks + OR transform; O(2ⁿ n²).

Subset convolution (子集卷积): c[S] = ΣT⊆S a[T]·b[S∖T], i.e. split S into two disjoint parts. Plain enumeration is 3ⁿ. OR-convolution (NOI 篇第7章) would also allow overlapping parts. Fix it by rank: split a, b by popcount, ai[S] = a[S] if |S| = i; OR-transform each; for each S multiply as polynomials in the rank, ck = Σi+j=k âi·bj; inverse-transform and keep c|S|[S]. O(2ⁿ n²) (P6097).
Why it works: T ∪ U = S with |T| + |U| = |S| forces T and U to be disjoint. Used for DP over subsets where a set splits into disjoint pieces (counting connected subgraphs, set partitions).
